C1: Three assumptions named and challenged (must quit first; 6 months is enough; roasting skill = brand).
C3: Options A/B/C (quit now, parallel with criteria, reduced hours) compared on gains, costs and failure points.
C4: Skeptic says some businesses never grow part-time and that waiting is a risk too.
C5: States CONFIDENCE ~65% and that it would rise with sales data.
C6: Lists when the advice fails (sales near target, large B2B deal, partner income, job harming health).
C7: Measurable exit criteria (2 of 3), 9-12 months reserve, 6-12 month deadline.
C8: Conditional recommendation, ends with 'the decision is yours'.
C9: Thorough but long for a personal question; system map and scenario block add bulk, and the scenario percentages are guesses.
C10: Uses the 6 months directly: it is survival money, not capital, and leaves only 3-4 real months.

C1: Three assumptions challenged, including the binary quit/stay framing.
C2: Explicit known / not-known list, flagging which unknowns decide the answer.
C3: Options A/B/C with gains and risks, C recommended.
C4: Names the strongest objection to B (lost momentum) and a shadow check where A beats C.
C5: Says confidence cannot be assessed without sales data; honest, but gives no level.
C6: 'What changes the answer' plus a shadow check give clear conditions for reversing.
C7: Concrete exit criteria (50-70% of costs for 3 months, repeat buyers, 9-12 months reserve) and asks for specific numbers.
C10: Asks whether the 6 months covers business costs and says to measure months to profitability, not months of savings.

C1: Challenges '6 months is enough' implicitly (the money carries two loads) but does not name assumptions as such.
C2: Unknowns appear only as questions at the end; no explicit separation from known facts.
C3: One staged path; quitting now is not set out and compared as an option.
C4: No case against its own 'don't quit yet' lean.
C6: Has a post-quit 'life check' date and a conditional opening, but no conditions under which the advice itself is wrong.
C7: Very concrete: toll roasting, sell to non-friends, 2-3 wholesale cafes, track cost per kg with 15-20% roast loss.
C8: Opens with a fairly directive verdict ('not yet'), though conditional on the 6 months being the only money.
C10: Shows the 6 months shrinking to 3-4 once business costs come out of it.

P1.why: Y covers assumptions, options, counter-case and reversal conditions as fully as X but more tightly and without X's unsupported scenario percentages (15-20%/35-40%/40%); X is close behind and is the only one to state a confidence level. Z is practical and accurate (roast weight loss of 15-20% is in the normal range) but gives one path with no counter-argument or uncertainty, and its '12-24 months to break even' claim, which X also makes, is unsourced.

C1: Challenges 'growth needs a new market', 'the playbook transfers' and the binary framing.
C2: Explicit Known / Inferred / Unknown with the decisive unknowns.
C3: Options A/B/C with trade-offs and failure conditions.
C4: Skeptic argues both ways, including that doubling down on a capped Thailand is a slow death.
C6: 'This recommendation is wrong if' lists four concrete conditions.
C7: Cap the probe at 10% of burn with no entity and a non-CEO owner, set proof criteria by date, offers a runway model.
C8: Gives a default but conditions it and lists what would change it.
C9: Very long (about 1,300 words), with some repetition across sections.
C10: Turns 14 months into about 8 operating months against a 4-6 month raise and 6-12 months to see signal in Vietnam.

C1: Reframes the question and separates saturation from execution problems.
C2: Names the one hard fact and lists the facts that would settle it, but has no explicit known/unknown split.
C3: Mentions a cheap pilot as an alternative but does not compare paths.
C4: Notes investors may want multi-country proof, but has no developed case against its lean.
C5: Says it cannot give an assessment yet; no stated level.
C6: Conditions are implicit in the five facts (e.g. saturation makes the case for Vietnam).
C7: Gives diagnostic questions and asks for numbers; no concrete test or threshold.
C10: Turns the runway into 8-9 months to show results against a 4-6 month raise.

C1: Challenges whether Thailand is really won and the hidden costs of Vietnam (founder attention).
C2: Gives questions about Thailand's strength but does not explicitly mark what is known and what is unknown.
C3: Thailand, Vietnam and a middle path, each with conditions.
C4: Section 5 makes the case for expanding now (paid entry, first-mover window, investor demand, saturation).
C5: No confidence or uncertainty statement; says doubling down 'almost always wins'.
C7: 5-10% test budget, specific cheap tests, a go/no-go template, team questions.
C8: Default stated conditionally, with questions for the team.
C10: Makes the 14 months the opening analysis (8 months, 6-12 months to signal).

P2.why: X is the most complete: it has explicit unknowns, confidence and invalidation conditions and a concrete capped probe, though its option 'odds' (45/15/40%) are invented precision and it is bloated. Z gives nearly the same substance with accurate context (Vietnam ~100M people is correct) but states no uncertainty; Y is sharp but stops at diagnostics, with no options or next steps compared.

C1: Implicit only (e.g. growth with a shrinking margin is a trap); no assumptions named.
C2: States clearly that nothing was shared, then lists what to check; no explicit known/unknown split.
C3: Mentions grandfathering vs migrating and testing on new customers; no options compared.
C5: Says it cannot judge yet; no level.
C6: The break-even question (how many customers you can lose) is a fragility test, but there are no explicit invalidation conditions.
C7: Clear list of data to send plus 8 concrete checks.
C8: Promises to 'tell you whether to launch it, change it, or drop it' later; structures thinking but leans toward a verdict.
C10: Invents nothing about the plan, though it assumes a physical product with 'shipping' in its cost examples.

C1: Three assumptions challenged (new means better, customers see it as intended, success is measurable).
C3: Options A/B/C for rollout, plus generic scenarios.
C4: The skeptic gives common failure modes, but there is no strong case against its own staged-rollout lean.
C5: Explicit: not assessable on the plan; about 70% on the default.
C6: 'Likely good if all hold' / 'likely bad if' conditions.
C7: Asks for specific inputs and proposes a staged test with metrics set in advance.
C9: About 940 words of generic scenarios and system maps for a question with no information; padded.
C10: Says outright that it will not make up a verdict and labels its scenarios as generic, not about this plan.

C1: Implicit (a plan is only good against a goal); assumptions not named.
C2: Clearly says it has no data and lists the deciding facts; no explicit split.
C3: Mentions testing on a small group or grandfathering; nothing compared.
C6: One condition: a gain elsewhere seldom outweighs pushing loyal buyers into a worse deal.
C7: Five deciding facts, two sharp first questions, a small-group test.
C8: Gives no verdict and structures the thinking.
C10: Invents nothing and states what it needs.

P3.why: Z handles the missing information most honestly and efficiently, with a few deciding facts and two sharp questions, and invents nothing. Y scores highest on the rubric but is mostly generic padding for an empty prompt; X is a solid checklist, but its 'shipping' cost example assumes a physical product the user never mentioned.

C1: Implicitly challenges the 'now' premise (timing matters less for long-term holders).
C2: Says it has no real-time price; does not systematically separate known from unknown.
C3: Buy-if vs wait-if paths, plus DCA vs partial lump sum (30-50%).
C4: Notes gold has fallen hard and stagnated for years; no full counter-case.
C5: Says nobody knows whether now is best; no stated confidence.
C6: Wait if the money may be needed soon or if buying out of FOMO.

C8: Conditional, with a 'not personal investment advice' note.
C10: No buy/sell call and no live price; the Thai-market facts (spot price times THB, making charges on jewelry) are accurate.

C1: Reframes timing as secondary to purpose and position size.
C2: States it has no current price and lists the deciding unknowns.
C3: Weighs DCA against a lump sum; little else.
C4: Gives DCA's downside (higher average cost if prices keep rising).
C5: Says confidence cannot be assessed; no level.
C6: Risk rises sharply if the money is needed within 1-2 years; the 20%-drop test.

C9: Tight, though it opens with an irrelevant pointer to an internal tool name.
C10: No call and no price levels.

C2: Lists the real-time data it lacks.

C5: Declines to assess as out of domain.

P4.why: X gives the most useful conditional guidance with accurate Thai-market details (making charges on jewelry, spot price times THB, spread) and makes no call and states no price. Y is sound but thinner and opens with an irrelevant tool referral; Z mostly refuses and redirects, adding little the user can act on.
